Trying to Conceive

How long does ovulation last, and when are you fertile?

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary. It is important for conception, but it is not a guaranteed monthly event or a process that always starts on cycle day 14. Understanding egg survival, sperm survival and the limits of tracking is more useful than treating one calendar date as certain.

What happens before and during ovulation?

Hormones coordinate the menstrual cycle. Follicles containing eggs develop in the ovaries, usually with one becoming dominant; an LH surge helps trigger release of its egg. Eggs are not newly created on particular cycle days. Development and release do not follow the same day-6-to-14 timetable for everyone.

Usually one egg is released; occasionally more than one is released around the same ovulatory episode, which can allow non-identical twins if both are fertilised. This does not mean there are separate predictable fertile windows throughout a cycle. After release, the egg can enter a fallopian tube, where fertilisation usually occurs if sperm meets it.

Egg release, egg survival and the fertile window

The release itself is an event, rather than a full day during which an egg keeps being released. An egg is generally able to be fertilised for about 12–24 hours after ovulation. If it is not fertilised, it breaks down; falling hormones later allow the uterine lining to shed as a period.

That short lifespan does not limit pregnancy to sex on one day. Sperm can remain capable of fertilisation for up to about five days in suitable reproductive-tract conditions. ASRM describes the main fertile window as the five days before ovulation plus the day of ovulation, with the highest chance often in the preceding one or two days. Because release time is uncertain and an egg may survive into the next day, do not use these estimates to declare any particular day safe from pregnancy.

If fertilisation occurs, the developing embryo travels towards the uterus and may implant in its lining several days later. Fertilisation and implantation are different events; neither happens reliably at a fixed hour after sex, and well-timed sex does not guarantee implantation or pregnancy.

When in the cycle does it happen?

Count cycle day 1 from the first day of menstrual bleeding. Day 14 is only a rough illustration for a 28-day cycle, not a rule for every person or every cycle. Ovulation commonly occurs roughly two weeks before the next period, with meaningful variation; you cannot know an exact future day simply by subtracting 14.

Regular cycles are often ovulatory, but even regular timing can vary and occasional cycles may not release an egg. Shorter, longer or irregular cycles make calendar estimates less dependable. Not everyone ovulates once in every calendar month, and bleeding alone does not prove ovulation.

Cervical mucus and other possible signs

Near the fertile part of the cycle, cervical mucus may become clearer, wetter, slippery and stretchy, sometimes like raw egg white. This can help identify days when conception is more likely, but it does not prove that an egg has been released; no obvious mucus change does not rule out pregnancy.

Some people notice mild cramps or one-sided discomfort, breast tenderness, bloating or a change in sexual desire; others notice nothing. These signs are nonspecific and cannot confirm the time of ovulation or diagnose pregnancy. New unusual discharge, unpleasant smell, itching or persistent pain deserves medical advice rather than being assumed to be a fertile sign.

Basal temperature and urine ovulation tests

Basal body temperature is measured at rest, usually on waking before activity. A small sustained rise can suggest that ovulation has already happened, so it is mainly retrospective, not an accurate advance signal for that cycle. Illness, sleep disruption and measurement differences can affect the record; some ovulatory cycles do not show a clear pattern.

Urine ovulation predictor kits detect an LH rise that often precedes ovulation by about one to two days. They predict rather than prove release, and false-positive or false-negative results occur, including misleading results with PMOS/PCOS. Follow the particular product’s timing and instructions; do not impose one testing time on every brand. A thermometer or test bought online is a tool, not a diagnosis or a guarantee of pregnancy.

Why ovulation may be irregular or absent

Possible causes include PMOS, previously called PCOS, thyroid dysfunction, high prolactin, the menopause transition, substantial weight or energy-balance changes, and excessive exercise. Significant stress can affect cycles in some people, but difficulty conceiving should not be blamed on failing to relax. Pregnancy and medicines or hormonal contraception also affect bleeding or ovulation, so assessment starts with your circumstances.

PCOS is now also called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), following the 2026 name change. It can affect ovulation, androgen-related hair or skin symptoms, metabolic health and mood; it is not simply an imbalance of oestrogen and progesterone creating harmless ovarian lumps. The small follicles that may appear on a scan are not the same as ordinary ovarian cysts, and a scan finding alone does not diagnose the syndrome.

Thyroid disease does not automatically mean early menopause

Both an overactive and an underactive thyroid can disturb periods and ovulation and make conception harder. Treatment may help when thyroid dysfunction is the cause. This is not the same as saying everyone with a thyroid problem will stop ovulating permanently or develop early menopause.

Autoimmune thyroid disease can sometimes occur alongside other autoimmune problems affecting ovarian function, but absent periods need assessment rather than an assumption of menopause. Tell the clinician about thyroid history, medicines and symptoms, and seek advice promptly when planning pregnancy or after a positive test if you have a known thyroid condition. Do not change thyroid treatment yourself.

Can bleeding happen without ovulation?

Yes. Hormonal changes can cause the uterine lining to bleed even without release of an egg. Such bleeding may be irregular, light, heavy or prolonged; it is not always a lighter or shorter normal period. A monthly-looking bleed is not absolute proof of ovulation, and one unusual cycle does not establish permanent infertility.

Seek assessment for a changed pattern, repeatedly very short or long cycles, absent periods, bleeding between periods, or bleeding lasting more than about a week. If pregnancy is possible, consider a pregnancy test and appropriate review. A clinician may select hormone tests or ultrasound when indicated, rather than everyone needing them or a universal “day-21” test.

Planning pregnancy and knowing when to ask for help

If you are trying to conceive, sex every two to three days through the cycle can cover an uncertain window without needing to identify an exact release time. Tracking can be optional help rather than a source of pressure; intercourse every one to two days in the fertile window is another approach if comfortable. Follow a fertility team’s own instructions if receiving treatment.

In general US guidance, seek fertility evaluation after 12 months of trying if under 35, after six months at 35 or older, and earlier around age 40 or above. Local pathways vary. Do not wait those intervals if periods are absent or markedly irregular, there is a known fertility-related condition, or another concern warrants assessment. When relevant, evaluation includes the partner providing sperm as well, rather than assuming all difficulty comes from ovulation.

Tracking is not a substitute for contraception or urgent care

A calendar, app, symptoms or a positive LH test alone cannot reliably mark safe days for avoiding pregnancy. Fertility-awareness contraception requires trained teaching and its own rules; it is less forgiving of errors and may be unsuitable with irregular cycles or when pregnancy must be avoided for health reasons. Use suitable contraception if pregnancy is not wanted; condoms also reduce STI risk.

Do not assume recurrent pelvic pain is ovulation pain without assessment, especially if pregnancy is possible. Severe or worsening abdominal/pelvic pain needs immediate emergency care even if it did not start suddenly. Pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain, faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding also needs immediate emergency care; do not drive yourself. With possible pregnancy, new one-sided pain needs urgent assessment now, even without a previous positive test or visible bleeding. Fever or abnormal discharge with pelvic pain also needs urgent advice.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

ACOG and ASRM distinguish the short egg lifespan from the longer fertile window; the ASRM 2022 and 2021 committee opinions remain available with their publication dates acknowledged.

ASRM describes the limits of calendar predictions, retrospective temperature changes and indirect urine LH testing; testing and fertility evaluation should be individualized.

June and July 2026 NHS information covers irregular cycles, PMOS terminology and assessment of concerning pelvic pain; thyroid disease is not a guarantee of early menopause.

NHS fertility-awareness information requires trained instruction for contraception and notes that apps are not officially recommended as contraceptive tools; this article does not identify safe days.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record cycle dates, symptoms, temperature or test observations and questions for a clinician. A record cannot confirm ovulation, diagnose a hormone disorder, guarantee pregnancy or provide reliable contraception. Do not delay care while collecting more cycles of data.

When to seek help

Do not assume recurrent pelvic pain is ovulation pain without assessment, especially if pregnancy is possible. Severe or worsening abdominal/pelvic pain needs immediate emergency care even if it did not start suddenly. Pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain, faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding also needs immediate emergency care; do not drive yourself. With possible pregnancy, new one-sided pain needs urgent assessment now, even without a previous positive test or visible bleeding. Fever or abnormal discharge with pelvic pain also needs urgent advice. Do not self-start fertility hormones or change thyroid medicines, and do not use calendar or test predictions alone to avoid pregnancy.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • An egg usually remains fertilisable for about 12–24 hours; the main fertile window is longer because sperm can survive for days.
  • Day 14 is an illustration, not a universal date, and regular bleeding does not guarantee ovulation in every cycle.
  • Mucus may help estimate fertility; temperature is mainly retrospective and LH tests predict rather than prove release.
  • PMOS/PCOS, thyroid problems and other conditions can affect ovulation; assessment is more useful than self-diagnosis or blame.
  • Use suitable contraception if pregnancy is not wanted, and seek urgent care for concerning pain rather than assuming ovulation.

Frequently asked questions

How long does ovulation last?

Release of the egg is an event. The egg generally survives for fertilisation for about 12–24 hours afterwards. The main fertile window includes several preceding days because sperm can survive in the reproductive tract.

Can I become pregnant from sex before ovulation?

Yes. Sperm may remain able to fertilise an egg for up to about five days in suitable conditions. The highest chance is often in the one or two days before release, but timing and conception are not guaranteed.

What are the most important signs?

Clear slippery stretchy mucus may suggest approaching fertility. A sustained basal-temperature rise is mainly evidence afterwards; cramps, breast tenderness, bloating or libido changes are nonspecific. No symptoms does not mean no ovulation.

How can I estimate the timing?

Combine awareness of your own cycle with optional mucus observations or an LH kit used according to its instructions. Temperature can help review past patterns. Apps, signs and kits do not identify an exact release time or establish that ovulation definitely occurred.

Can thyroid disease prevent ovulation?

An overactive or underactive thyroid can interfere with ovulation and periods, but does not automatically cause early menopause. Seek assessment and individualized treatment rather than changing thyroid medicine yourself.

Can I bleed without ovulating?

Yes. Hormonal changes may cause bleeding without egg release, and it may be light, heavy, prolonged or irregular. Persistent changes or absent periods need assessment; bleeding alone cannot prove ovulation.

When should I seek fertility advice?

Common US guidance is 12 months under age 35, six months at 35 or older, and earlier around 40 or above. Seek advice sooner with absent or markedly irregular periods or a known fertility-related condition; local referral pathways differ.

Can I use these estimates to avoid pregnancy?

Do not rely on a predicted day or LH test alone. Fertility-awareness contraception requires professional teaching and specific rules, and may be unsuitable for you. Choose appropriate contraception; condoms also help prevent STIs.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
